rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs. The high final organic fraction reduces the risk of unobserved late compounds.
Test a substantial temperature change at the same gradient to reveal selectivity shifts in the crowded middle cluster and late pair. All peaks currently elute well before the time penalty begins.

Use a shallower gradient to spread the nearly coeluting peaks and test gradient-dependent selectivity at the better-performing temperature. The current elution window leaves substantial room for improvement before 10 minutes.
Keep the shallower gradient that resolved the middle cluster and lower temperature by 5 C to shift the remaining coeluting pair. The last peak has some margin below the 10-minute penalty threshold.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shift gradient selectivity while retaining the favorable 55 C separation of the later peaks. This also provides more time margin for resolving the remaining critical pair with a shallower gradient.

At 60 C the middle cluster was fully resolved, leaving only a later coelution. A shallower gradient with a higher starting organic fraction tests whether that pair can separate while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes.

Further reduce the gradient slope to improve the remaining late-pair resolution at 60 C. Raising the starting organic fraction should offset the longer gradient and keep the last peak below 10 minutes, while testing whether the earlier separations remain adequate.

Use an intermediate starting organic fraction to recover the early-cluster separation lost in injection 7, while retaining a shallow gradient for the late critical pair. This balances the complementary strengths of injections 6 and 7.

Test the cold end of the temperature range for a different selectivity pattern, since 55–60 C trades one critical pair against another. A moderately faster gradient should limit late-peak time penalties while revealing whether cooling separates the middle cluster.
Injection 9 reached the maximum CRF. Shorten the gradient by one step to seek a faster fully resolved method while retaining injection 9 as the benchmark.

Restore the 20-minute gradient that gave full resolution, but raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten retention. The narrower gradient window may preserve the critical-pair separation better than shortening tG alone.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to lift the remaining R = 1.40 pair above 1.5. The last peak at 8.75 minutes leaves room for this adjustment while potentially retaining a faster fully resolved separation than injection 9.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shorten retention while lowering the final fraction to protect critical-pair resolution with a shallower slope. Injection 12 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.

Lower the final organic fraction one step to improve the sole unresolved pair from injection 13. This modest slope reduction may restore full resolution with the last peak still earlier than injection 12.
Raise temperature one step from the fastest fully resolved method to test whether retention can be shortened without losing critical-pair resolution. Keep injection 14 as the fully resolved fallback.

Test whether another 5 C increase moves the late pair beyond its near-coelution while further shortening retention. Monitor the early cluster closely because its separations were near the acceptance threshold at 30 C.

Return to the temperature with demonstrated full resolution and test a higher starting organic fraction for faster elution. A substantially narrower gradient window aims to compensate for the critical-pair resolution lost when the starting fraction increases.

Refine around injection 14 with a slightly steeper slope of 0.025 organic fraction per minute versus 0.02593 here. This should shorten retention while testing whether its R = 1.61 critical pair retains full resolution.

Test a slope of 0.03409, between injections 11 and 12, to target full resolution with shorter retention. Injection 18 actually had the same slope as injection 14, so it did not provide the intended slope refinement.
Test a 5 C increase from the fully resolved injection 12 to seek a faster maximum-score method. The lower starting fraction and steeper slope than injection 15 may avoid its late-pair overlap.

With the maximum CRF already secured, test a faster, higher-organic regime that may separate the critical middle pair after an elution-order crossover. Injection 19 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved fallback.

Lengthen the promising fast gradient by one step to improve the R = 1.41 pair and protect the late pair at R = 1.57. This could deliver full resolution far sooner than the current maximum-score methods.

Use a slope of 0.050, between injections 21 and 22, to shorten the fully resolved separation while targeting R above 1.5 for both critical pairs. Injection 22 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method.

Test one step higher starting organic fraction for faster elution, with a shallower slope to help preserve resolution. Injection 23 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method if this compresses a critical pair too much.

Return to the fastest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature by one step to test for further time savings without sacrificing resolution. Injection 23 remains the preferred demonstrated method if this final adjustment lowers CRF.
